title: Feature request: fallback to a default `code_highlight()` theme if RStudio theme is unavailable
description:
If you try to use `code_highlight()` in RStudio when using a theme that is not included in `code_theme_list()`, you receive a warning message and the code is returned unhighlighted:
```r
cli::code_highlight("1 + 1")
#> [1] "1 + 1"
#> Warning message:
#> In code_theme_default_rstudio() :
#>   cli does not know this RStudio theme: a11y-dark {rsthemes}
```

It would be preferable to fallback to a default theme if `cli` does not recognize the current RStudio theme: perhaps to `cli:::code_theme_default_term()` or "Textmate (default)".
The warning message could be preserved and could also indicate that the user can choose a code highlighting theme using `options()`.

title: Add `style_hyperlink_run()`?
Text in the rules (cli_rule and cat_rule)
description:
### Introduction *** Hi! I want to color my rules, but I don't need to color the text inside the rule. It doesn't look very good, in my and my colleagues' opinion. So, I have to color the text in the standard letter color of the current RStudio theme, but there is a big problem.
### Problem *** In my working practice, different people use different RStudio themes, dark, white and others (rarely, but they also occur). And I have to write a lot of ugly add-ons to handle these cases, while they work poorly, some themes return me incorrect information about the color of the main letters in `rstudioapi::getThemeInfo()`, and also, for example, the pure white color `"#000000"` is not as bright as the RStudio theme: ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52919010/184113362-fca7ea4e-137d-4392-b2d5-ef5c6d37d1c6.png) Especially a lot of problems arise when I have to parse the saved text in a log file with cli coloring back to the console in another RStudio theme. I used a white theme on my car, and a black one on someone else's car. Or if the script was run from under linux without rstudioapi - it is also not clear what color to paint.
### Request *** Please make sure that `cli_rule` and `cat_rule` color the text in the standard color of the letters of the current RStudio theme, and the color of the RULE does not affect the text in it. I.e., isolate the line color from the text color. It will look normal and work correctly. If I need to colorize the text in the rule, I can define it. But in my practice - I do not have such an opportunity.

title: Adding linebreaks inside {.code <code>} causes a vapply error
description:
I was looking to nicely display some code with line breaks, and writing something like so I got this `vapply` error:

``` r
cat(
  cli::format_error(
    message = c(
      "error",
      "do this:",
      "{.code

      x = 1:10,
      )}"

  )
)

#>  but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 3

# adding in \n didn't work
cat(
  cli::format_error(
    message = c(
      "error",
      "do this:",
      "{.code \nmean(\n\nx = 1:10\n)}"
    )
  )
)

cat(
  cli::format_error(
    message = c(
      "error",
      "do this:",
      "{.code \fmean(\fx = 1:10\f)}"
    )
  )
)
```

title: `cli::cli_inform()` vs `rlang::inform()`
description:
In our project, we use `{cli}` for user notification. I am looking into adopting newest versions of `{cli}` and `{rlang}`. 
I noticed failing snapshot test that showed that each time we output a message using `cli::cli_inform()`, I get an extra blank line before the printed message (*in the snapshot*). So if I run
```R
cli::cli_inform(text, class = class, .envir = env)
```
I get extra blanks. However, if I replace it with `{rlang}`, I get correct output
```R
rlang::inform(purrr::map_chr(text, cli::format_inline, .envir = env), class = class, call = env)
```
(I know these two calls are not identical operations)

Here is a diff of the snapshot we get while testing, note extra blank lines.

Q: How to preserve "everything" in an active sink?
description:
Hi. My question is basically:

- Which options should be set, and to what values, for **cli** to behave identically inside an active sink as outside?

As the below example shows, I figured out that I need to set options `cli.num_colors = cli::num_ansi_colors()` to preserver colors.  Are there other options one need to consider to preserve "everything" that **cli** can output via stdout and conditions.

```r
library(cli)
cli_test <- function() {
  cli_alert_danger("watch out\n")
}

# Default without active sink
options(cli.num_colors = NULL)
cli_test()
#> ✖ watch out   # ✖ in RED

# Default with active sink
options(cli.num_colors = NULL)
void <- utils::capture.output(cli_test())
#> ✖ watch out   # No colors

# Preserve colors with active sink
options(cli.num_colors = cli::num_ansi_colors())
void <- utils::capture.output(cli_test())
#> ✖ watch out   # ✖ in RED
```

This is with cli 3.2.0 with R 4.1.2 running in a Linux terminal.

```r
library(tibble)
mtcars
as_tibble(mtcars)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4790348/153068849-438e4a4d-e46a-4608-a9eb-2bfcdb936191.png)


I am experiencing this with all packages that use `cli`, e.g., `devtools`, `tidyverse`, `targets`, etc. and it occurs consistently on multiple computers. It would be great to see this fixed. The current vscode-R suggestion is to use a different R terminal (radian) but there are a number of reasons why a user would not want to use an R terminal that depends on python and conda.

title: Add a ruler
description:
```R
ruler <- function(width = getOption("width")) {
  x <- seq_len(width)
  y <- case_when(
    x %% 10 == 0 ~ as.character((x %/% 10) %% 10),
    x %% 5 == 0  ~ "+",
    TRUE         ~ "-"
  )
  cat(y, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(x %% 10, "\n", sep = "")
}

ruler()
```

This is super useful for debugging font issues in latex and html

description:
The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt

title: Global option to disable unicode in condition bullets
description:
This option should only be inspected when `cli.unicode` is enabled. I.e. it's a way of opting out of unicode in condition message bullets when unicode is globally enabled, not opting in when it's globally disabled.

This way reproducible environments only need to disable `cli.unicode` without having to know about condition bullets. On the other hand, unit tests that specifically enable unicode will need to know about the bullets-specific option for reproducibility in sessions where the user has disabled unicode bullets, but that's a rare case.

I think the name should be nested in `cli.unicode_`, mention bullets, and mention that it's about condition messaging. One of these would be good:

- `cli.unicode_cnd_bullets`
- `cli.unicode_condition_bullets`
- `cli.unicode_message_bullets`

Or perhaps nest in `cli.unicode_bullets_` in case similar options are added for bullets in other contexts?

title: logging info or verbose control support
description:
Hi rlib team,

Thanks for developing this nice tool. I am wondering if this tool can support a switch for verbose control. It's very common to set a `verbose` in functions of an R package. If I implement this in my own, it will end up many `if` checks in functions with many `cli_*` like:

```R
if (getOptions("package.verbose")) cli_alert_info(...)
```

I don't know if there could be a global control that all `cli_*` functions can identify it.

e.g.

```
f = function(x, y, z, verbose = TRUE) {
  if (verbose) set_cli_verbose(TRUE)
 
  # Now all cli_* function will auto detect the cli_verbose and decide if print message
  cli_alert_info(...)
  cli_alert_warn(...)
  ...
}
```

Go further, there could be a logging level like 1, 2, 3 to control different print levels.

Best,

Shixiang

title: Integrate with RStudio Jobs API
description:
When I use `progress` in the RStudio IDE it works swimmingly. But if I source the script as a Job, I don't see the progress bar (presumably because it's not an interactive session or some such.)

It would be cool if we could integrate `progress` with `rstudioapi::jobSetProgress()` so that we could still use the same function to update progress and see it on the top-level job instead of on stderr.

title: How to harden the formatting of URLs? (issue with `#` encoding)
description:
I came across an edge case where some URLs are not rendering as expected.

Here's a minimal reprex:

```r
## From googlesheets4 vignette:
## https://googlesheets4.tidyverse.org/articles/googlesheets4.html

url <- "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1U6Cf_qEOhiR9AZqTqS3mbMF3zt2db48ZP5v3rkrAEJY/edit#gid=780868077"

cli::cli_alert(sprintf("Downloading '%s'.", url))
## → Downloading 'https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1U6Cf_qEOhiR9AZqTqS3mbMF3zt2db48ZP5v3rkrAEJY/edit#gid=780868077'.

cli::cli_alert(sprintf("Downloading {.file %s}.", url))
## → Downloading

cli::cli_alert(sprintf("Downloading {.url %s}.", url))
## → Downloading

cli::cli_alert(sprintf("Downloading {.val %s}.", url))
## → Downloading

cli::cli_alert(sprintf("Downloading {.var %s}.", url))
## → Downloading
```

Is there a way to harden the encoding of URLs to work better with the cli package?

title: Unexpected indenting or truncation of messages
description: I have noticed that some of my messages are unexpectedly indented or truncated. I have found it hard to reproduce so possibly it is something specific to my setup (RStudio on MacOS). It's also possible I'm just doing something incorrectly, just let me know if that's the case. Here are the conditions that seem to reproduce for me: 1. Call `cli_process_start()` with a relatively long message 2. Call `cli_progress_step()` with a field in the message 3. Call one of the `cli_alert()` functions ``` r f <- function() { cli::cli_process_start( "A main process with a long message saying what it is doing" ) cli::cli_progress_step("Some intermediate step with a {.field field}") cli::cli_alert_warning("An alert messsage which is long enough") } f() #> ℹ A main process with a long message saying what it is doing #> ℹ Some intermediate step with a field #> ! An alert messsage which is long enough #> ℹ Some intermediate step with a field✓ Some intermediate step with a field [19ms] #> #> ℹ A main process with a long message saying what it is doing✓ A main process with a long message saying what it is doing ... done ``` Created on 2021-09-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1) It doesn't seem to happen in the reprex which is annoying but what I see is the `cli_progress_step()` message is indented. Sometimes instead of this happening the `cli_alert()` message is truncated which I think is probably a worse effect. I realise this is probably a weird edge case so totally understand if you don't want to spend time on it but thought I would open an issue in case it comes up for anyone else.

title: Integer overflow when using the C progress bar API
description:
When using the C progress bar API it is possible to overflow the 32 bit `int` data type if you pass a value larger than can be stored in an `int`, e.g. more than 2147483647.

In my case I was trying to use the `download` progress bar type and simply passing the number of bytes read so far to `cli_progress_set()` with a ~ 3 Gb file.

Would it be possible for the functions accept a wider integer type like `int64_t` or `size_t` to avoid this issue for most real world integers?

title: double clic_unload
description:
I've run into an interesting bug that manifests as:

```
Error in .Call(clic_unload) : NULL value passed as symbol address
```

In essence, what appears to be happening is that if one unloads the `cli` namespace, then `clic_unload` is invoked via `.onUnload`, but then at a later point if the namespace is gc'ed, the entry point is called again while being possibly in a corrupted state.

As I noted I cannot reproduce the actual error simply, but I did modify `cli` to show when it's running `clic_unload`:

```
--- a/R/onload.R
+++ b/R/onload.R
@@ -57,7 +57,11 @@ task_callback <- NULL
   )
 
   # For valgrind: https://github.com/r-lib/cli/issues/311
-  reg.finalizer(asNamespace("cli"), function(x) .Call(clic_unload), TRUE)
+  reg.finalizer(
+      asNamespace("cli"), 
+      function(x) {message("finalizer");.Call(clic_unload)},
+      TRUE
+  )
 
   if (getRversion() >= "3.5.0") {
     `__cli_update_due` <<- .Call(clic_make_timer);
@@ -141,6 +145,7 @@ task_callback <- NULL
   tryCatch(removeTaskCallback(task_callback), error = function(e) NULL)
   tryCatch(cli_progress_cleanup(), error = function(e) NULL)
   tryCatch(ansi_show_cursor(), error = function(e) NULL)
+  message("unload")
   .Call(clic_unload)
 }
```

With that patch I can then create this session transcript:

```
vagrant@vagrant:/vagrant/trunk$ ./bin/R --no-restore --quiet
> loadNamespace('cli')
<environment: namespace:cli>
> unloadNamespace('cli')
unload
> q()
Save workspace image? [y/n/c]: n
finalizer
```

I have not been able to trigger the finalizer simply (e.g. by running `gc(full=TRUE)`) and obviously the above does not show the error, but it does show `clic_unload` being run _after_ the namespace is unloaded, which seems dangerous.  In some of my testing I got a segfault, but again in nothing simple enough to be reproducible, so I am not certain that `cli` is responsible.

The actual error occurred in the context of tests being run with `test_dir`, with code that attempts to unload most loaded packages.

There is no need to address this issue for me as I'm working around it.  Possibly related to #311 and #318.

title: Width of heading separators too great, causing wrapping in RStudio
description: The width of the `─` character, when printed in RStudio console, is greater than the standard single width, causing the message to be wrapped, and thus not very neat. This applies at least to `cli_h1()` and `cli_rule()` on a Mac. Below are two representations of some output. * First a screenshot, this shows the wrapping clearly: * Then the actual text that got printed out, wrapped in code fences, compared to the same number of regular dashes. This seems to result in correct width when I view it in the browser: ``` ── x ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── -- x --------------------------------------------------------------------------- ``` This is probably affected by the font that is in use, but I've tested it with `Consolas`, `Inconsolata` and `Courier`, and I always get this issue, making me thing that the glyph that is being used is not guaranteed to be standard-width even in fixed width fonts (although I found that it does work in some other fonts, such as `Menlo`). The issue seems closely related to #91. I'm not sure what the most appropriate fix is. In the readme I don't see any emphasis on which typeface to use with `cli`, making me think that the intention is to be relatively agnostic about the typeface, but in this case it is quite sensitive to the font. If a better glyph is not available, should there be a prominent notice discussing which fonts have been tested and are supported?

title: Using `cli_progress_bar()` in parallel
description:
Is it possible (in principle or in practice) to use cli progress bars with parallel computation?

I'd like to be able to write:

```r
library("parallel")
env <- environment()
cli_progress_bar("Example", total = 10, .envir = env)
cl <- makeCluster(2)
parLapply(cl, 1:10, function (i, env) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  cli::cli_progress_update(1,  .envir = env)
}, env)
stopCluster(cl)
```

but I see
` Cannot find current progress bar for <environment: R_GlobalEnv>`


Is the parent environment accessible to workers?  Or am I doing something silly?

title: Better  CLI_TICK_TIME defaults for dynamic terminals?
description:
Animation update timer in as of version `3.0.0` defaults  to use 200ms in interactive sessions and 3s in non-interactive sessions. The tools I am developing are non-interactive, but they are primarily run in a dynamic terminal, where these defaults result in laggy animations. It is possible to modify the default via the `CLI_TICK_TIME` environmental variable, but that's not the most convenient way of doing things. This variable has to be set before `cli` is loaded, which makes using it awkward. For example, one can't  use `is_dynamic_tty()` to check if the terminal is dynamic (as that would load the package and use the default values). Or, if a user has an `.Rprofile` that loads `cli` on startup, manipulating the variable at the beginning of my script won't have any effect. And setting `CLI_TICK_TIME` in the shell creates issues with user experience. 

Since it seems that dynamic discovery of timer interval would be too complicated, may I suggest that the shorter update interval is chosen for interactive **and** dynamic sessions? This would solve all the current problems with animations in rich terminals. The change would be trivial:

https://github.com/r-lib/cli/blob/08695e486eb5630eb350086f0eb905223ffcf7e6/R/onload.R#L44

```diff
-    tt <- if (interactive()) {
+    tt <- if (interactive() || is_dynamic_tty() ) {
```

title: div margins do not clear status lines
description:
If a `div` is active with a top or bottom margin, an active process's status bar will not be cleared when the div is printed.

```r
library(cli)  # tested on v2.5.0, @8560ac3

example_cli_output <- function() {
  cli_process_start("active process")

  d <- cli::cli_div(theme = list("." = list("margin-left" = 4L)))
  cli_text("div text with only a left margin")
  cli_end(d)

  cli_alert("alert")

  d <- cli::cli_div(theme = list("." = list("margin-left" = 4L, "margin-top" = 1L, "margin-bottom" = 1L)))
  cli_text("div text with a top and bottom margin")
  cli_end(d)

  cli_alert("alert")
  cli_process_done()
}

example_cli_output()
#     div text with only a left margin
# → alert
# ℹ active process
#     div text with a top and bottom margin
# ℹ active process
# → alert
# ✔ active process ... done
```

The `ℹ active process` lines are expected to be empty, leaving room for the `div` margins

title: Purpose of random_id() in make_cmd_transformer()?
description:
## Preface
This post is not so much about a bug but rather a question about some (to me) unexpected behavior `cli` causes when calling `readr::read_csv()`. If this is not the best place to ask such a question (because, again, this is probably not a bug), please direct me to a more suitable place to ask my question. The original question can be found on [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/67909394/what-does-read-csv-use-random-numbers-for) (this also includes a reprex and an incomplete explanation of why this is happening).

## Problem
I recently came to realize that using `readr::read_csv()` uses random numbers which of course is somewhat unexpected behavior for a function that simply reads data. On [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/67909394/what-does-read-csv-use-random-numbers-for) someone was kind enough to point out that  `readr::read_csv()` uses the `cli` package whose function `random_id()` [here](https://github.com/r-lib/cli/blob/55028b16f1b7a0b98f8d152ddf01f1200917d713/R/inline.R#L214) uses random numbers.  So, for completeness' sake, I would like to understand what the purpose of `random_id()` is. 

## Reprex from Stackoverflow (for completeness)

```
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(123)
rnorm(1)
# [1] -0.5604756

set.seed(123)
dat <- read.csv("data/titanic.csv")
rnorm(1)
# [1] -0.5604756

set.seed(123)
dat <- read_csv("data/titanic.csv")
rnorm(1)
```

- In Rterm (run r.exe from cmd), the spinner characters are shown as "<U+xxxx>".

I first thought the Rterm problem is because Windows Command Line console couldn't show Unicode. title: Possible `cli_memo()` refinements
description: I've compared `cli_memo()` to some of my homegrown workarounds that pre-dated the addition of `cli_memo()`. And I'm also comparing `cli_memo()` to `cli_alert()` (and friends) and `rlang::abort()`. For consistency, it seems like a few tweaks might make sense. --- ## Indentation (or, rather, doing less indentation) Proposal: Don't indent the items, at least, in general / by default. Here's a simplified version of my `reprex_path()` helper, based on the workaround we worked out elsewhere. ``` r reprex_path <- function(header, path, .envir = parent.frame()) { cli::cli_alert_success(header, wrap = TRUE, .envir = .envir) cli::cli_div(theme = list(.alert = list(`margin-left` = 2, before = ""))) cli::cli_alert("{.path {path}}") cli::cli_end() } reprex_file <- tempfile() reprex_path("Writing reprex file:", reprex_file) #> ✓ Writing reprex file: #> /tmp/Rtmp5jcukq/filef99d16744a8e ``` Here's the closest I can come with `cli:memo()`. I need to un-indent the first line. ``` r cli::cli_memo(c(v = "Writing reprex file:", " " = "{.path {reprex_file}}")) #> ✓ Writing reprex file: #> /tmp/Rtmp5jcukq/filef99d16744a8e ``` I'm proposing that these two calls produce the same output: ``` r cli::cli_alert_success("alert success!") #> ✓ alert success! cli::cli_memo(c(v = "memo success!")) #> ✓ memo success! ```

title: tree() throws warning if passed a tibble
description:
The `cli::tree()` function throws a (presumably) undesirable warning if it's passed a tibble instead of a data frame (presumably, a likely use case). It's caused by https://github.com/r-lib/cli/blob/bc066c1c429b4e4d4dceb6bda6cb1bd15db57877/R/tree.R#L117
where `data$trimmed` returns `NULL` as expected but also a warning if `data` is a tibble. There are numerous obvious, easy ways to work around that, so I won't bother suggesting a solution/PR.

``` r
data <- data.frame(
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  package = c("A", "B", "C"),
  dependencies = c("B", "C", "")
)

cli::tree(data)
#> A
#> └─B
#>   └─C

cli::tree(tibble::as_tibble(data))
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `trimmed`.
#> A
#> └─B
#>   └─C

data$trimmed
#> NULL

tibble::as_tibble(data)$trimmed
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `trimmed`.
#> NULL
```

title: Justification
description:
I have a format method need in several places that's hard to express in cli's semantic UI interface. It basically looks like this:

``` r
x <- list(
  "<package>"     = "googledrive",
  "<app>"         = "tidyverse-app",
  "<api_key>"     = "123...xyz",
  "<auth_active>" = TRUE,
  "<credentials>" = "TokenServiceAccount"
)

fr <- function(x) format(x, justify = 'right')
fl <- function(x) format(x, justify = 'left')

cli::cli_h1("<AuthState (via {.pkg gargle})>")
#> 
#> ── <AuthState (via gargle)> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
glue::glue("{fr(names(x))} {fl(x)}")
#>     <package> googledrive
#>         <app> tidyverse-app
#>     <api_key> 123...xyz
#> <auth_active> TRUE
#> <credentials> TokenServiceAccount
```

<sup>Created on 2021-03-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0.9002)</sup>

This is hard to express with cli, due to:

* Justification / whitespace preservation
* Vectorization

What I wish I could say is more like this fictional `cli::cli_key_value()` function:

```
AuthState <- R6::R6Class("AuthState", list(
  ...,
  format = function(...) {
    x <- list(
      "<package>"     = "{.pkg {self$pkg}}",
      "<app>"         = "{.field {self$app}}",
      "<api_key>"     = "{.secret {self$api_key}}",
      "<auth_active>" = "{.val self$auth_active}}",
      "<credentials>" = "{.class {class(self$credentials)[[1]])}}"
    )
    cli::cli_format_method({
      cli::cli_h1("<AuthState (via {.pkg gargle})>")
      cli::cli_key_value(x)
    })
  }
))
```

Is this completely out of scope? The idea of having some control over whitespace seems related to #211. It feels like an open question is how (if?) to combine the semantic UI with affording some control over line breaks or "field width".

title: Add a `cli_glue` type function to the package?
description:
I've now had several packages where it is necessary to construct a text string using cli formatting in a different scope from where the message will eventually be printed for the user. I find it very helpful to be able to use the inline text formatting in these cases but I don't have an obvious way of restructuring the code so that this can be contained within a `cli_text` or similar call. 

For these packages I've added a simple function along the lines of 
```r
cli_glue = function(..., .envir = parent.frame()) {
  txt = cli::cli_format_method(cli::cli_text(..., .envir = .envir))
  # cli_format_method does wrapping which we dont want at this stage so glue things back together.
  paste(txt, collapse = " ")
}
```
This seems like a common enough use case that it potentially belongs in the package?  It also seems like it might be useful in the context of #142 and seems inline with the addition of the `pluralize` function.

title: Nesting `cli_ul` and/or `cli_ol`
description:
Currently it appears that both of these list interfaces only support at most two levels of nesting. See the examples below for either ul, ol, or mixed cases:


``` r
test_ul = function(n = 2) {
  for(i in seq_len(n)) {
    cli::cli_ul()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",i))
  }
}

test_ul(2)
#> ● Level 1
#>   ◯ Level 2
test_ul(3)
#> ● Level 1
#>   ◯ Level 2
#>   ─ Level 3
test_ul(4)
#> ● Level 1
#>   ◯ Level 2
#>   ─ Level 3
#>   ─ Level 4
```

```r
test_ol = function(n = 2) {
  for(i in seq_len(n)) {
    cli::cli_ol()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",i))
  }
}

test_ol(2)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
test_ol(3)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
#>   1. Level 3
test_ol(4)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
#>   1. Level 3
#>   1. Level 4
```

```r
test_ol_ul = function(n = 2) {
  for(i in seq_len(n)) {
    cli::cli_ol()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",2*i-1))
    
    cli::cli_ul()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",2*i))
  }
}

test_ol_ul(1)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   ● Level 2
test_ol_ul(2)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   ● Level 2
#>   1. Level 3
#>   ◯ Level 4
test_ol_ul(3)
#> 1. Level 1
#>   ● Level 2
#>   1. Level 3
#>   ◯ Level 4
#>   1. Level 5
#>   ─ Level 6
```

```r
test_ul_ol = function(n = 2) {
  for(i in seq_len(n)) {
    cli::cli_ul()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",2*i-1))
    
    cli::cli_ol()
    cli::cli_li(paste0("Level ",2*i))
  }
}

test_ul_ol(1)
#> ● Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
test_ul_ol(2)
#> ● Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
#>   ◯ Level 3
#>   1. Level 4
test_ul_ol(3)
#> ● Level 1
#>   1. Level 2
#>   ◯ Level 3
#>   1. Level 4
#>   ─ Level 5
#>   1. Level 6
```

title: cli & testthat messages - suppressed ansi codes
description:
I've been trying to add output to a testthat expectation message using the captured output of an object that uses cli for formatting. For some reason the testthat "enivornment" seems to suppress utf8 and ansi by default. The former I can avoid via `options(cli.unicode = TRUE)` but the latter I cannot seem to solve at the moment. 

I've tried both `options(cli.ansi = TRUE)` and `options(cli.dynamic = TRUE)` but both result in the same output. A quick example test file that shows this:

```r
expect_test = function() {

  withr::local_options(cli.unicode = TRUE, cli.ansi = TRUE, cli.dynamic = TRUE)

  msg = paste(
    cli::style_bold("hello"),
    cli::col_red("1...2...3..."),
    "Goodbye",
    sep="\n"
  )

  exp = expectation("failure", msg, srcref = NULL, trace = NULL)
  exp_signal(exp)

  invisible()
}


test_that("test test", {
  expect_equal(1,1)
  expect_equal(1,2)
  expect_test()
  expect_test()
  expect_equal(1,1)
})
```

Inspecting the `msg` object shows that the `hello` and `1...2...3...` never get the proper ansi codes added.

title: install.packages('cli') from `source` or `binary` and 'pkgbuild' dependencies
description:
It looks as if 'cli' package installation fails because package 'cli' is not available/installed? 
Running R-4.0.4 on CMD line with `R --vanilla` on Windows 10 PRO 20H2.   
Originally I ran into this during `update.packages()`   
Then I fiddled around with `remove.packages('cli')` plus remove.packages('pkgbuild')` because of some dependecies between those two. 
sort of then trying a fresh `cli` package installation.   
R the seems to default to `type = 'source'` below and throws the described `loadNamespace- Error`   

```
There is a binary version available but the source version is later:
    binary source needs_compilation
cli  2.3.0  2.3.1             FALSE

installing the source package 'cli'

trying URL 'https://cran.wu.ac.at/src/contrib/cli_2.3.1.tar.gz'
Content type 'application/x-gzip' length 134171 bytes (131 KB)
downloaded 131 KB

Error in loadNamespace(j <- i[[1L]], c(lib.loc, .libPaths()), versionCheck = vI[[j]]) :
  there is no package called 'cli'
Calls: local ... loadNamespace -> withRestarts -> withOneRestart -> doWithOneRestart
Execution halted

The downloaded source packages are in
        'C:\Users\userid\AppData\Local\Temp\RtmpAhV2it\downloaded_packages'
Warning message:
In install.packages("cli") :
  installation of package 'cli' had non-zero exit status
```
Workaround solution: `install.packages('cli', type = 'binary')` which will install version `2.3.0` BUT because of inter-dependencies between `cli` and `pkgbuild` (pkgbuild importing cli, therefore cannot unload) updating cli even with fresh restart of `R --vanilla` and neither cli nor pkgbuild showing up in `search()` runs into ` namespace 'cli' is imported by 'pkgbuild' so cannot be unloaded` issues. 
Is this expected/intentional behaviour?

title: Importance of the cli app should be much more obvious
description:
A companion issue to https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/1296 based on reprex's recent switch to testthat 3e (including snapshot tests of user-facing messaging) and the use of cli for the UI. 

I had a very tough time getting saved snapshots that did **not** contain Unicode and ANSI escapes.

This PR https://github.com/tidyverse/reprex/pull/351 in reprex shows the problem. The use of Unicode and ANSI colours by cli inside a test is, by default, **not** under the control of the current values of seemingly relevant options, nor is it under the control of whatever `cli::cli_sitrep()` reports.

Instead, if a cli "app" happens to already be running, *its* state is what matters. It's hard to predict what causes the cli app to start. From https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/pull/1295 in testthat, it seems one is not running prior to the first snapshot test involving cli, but https://github.com/tidyverse/reprex/pull/351 in reprex shows the opposite. Does it have something to do with the nature of the cli calls inside the package?

How did I know to bark up the "app" tree? Conversing with @hadley elsewhere about my frustrations, he suggested that I explicitly call `cli::start_app()` in the affected tests (the ones snapshotting code that contains cli calls) and this resolved the problem.

Possible things to do in cli:

* More documentation around the existence of cli apps and their significance. Which cli functions are influenced by the app and which are not? What causes an app to start and set its Unicode/colour state?
* It feels like `cli::cli_sitrep()` should report the settings actually in force and, perhaps, reflect *why* they are in force. Or report these options AND whether an app is running and what its settings are.
* Recommend the use of `cli::start_app(.auto_close = TRUE)` in any test that calls cli, where there are expectations about the cli output (it's possible that `testthat::test_that()` will take care of this).

title: has_color is not well detected in condition message
description:
This follows some investigations to close https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1805 with an issue in rlang error coloring when rendering an Rmd file. 

See the last reprex at https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1805#issuecomment-581146557

It seems `has_color` does not return the same result depending how the error message is created.

See this Rmd results 

<details><summary>Rmd source</summary>

````r
---
title: "crayon in Rmd"
output: md_document
---
Check some `has_color` success conditions
```{r}
crayon_sitrep <- function() {
  paste(
    "\n",
    "crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() :", 
    crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support(), "\n",
    "sink.number() :", sink.number(), "\n",
    "isatty(stdout()) :", isatty(stdout())
  )
}
```

Building error this way, `sink.number > 0` so result is not TRUE even in RStudio

```{r, error = TRUE}
er <- errorCondition(
  message = crayon_sitrep())
stop(er)
```

However, using a specific class for a condition and definining a special method
for `conditionMessage`, `sink.number()` is equal to 0 (reset ?) and `has_color` 
see RStudio is used. That why we get TRUE for color support. 

```{r, error = TRUE}
conditionMessage.barfoo <- function(c) crayon_sitrep()
stop(errorCondition("", class = "barfoo"))
```

## With rlang

This above is causing issue with rlang error too,and thus the tidyverse in
Rmarkdown.

```{r, error = TRUE}
rlang::abort(crayon_sitrep())
```

```{r, error = TRUE}
conditionMessage.foobar <- function(cnd) crayon_sitrep()
rlang::abort(.subclass = "foobar")
```
````
</details>

<details><summary>Resulting markdown output with results</summary>

Check some `has_color` success conditions

```r
crayon_sitrep <- function() {
  paste(
    "\n",
    "crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() :", 
    crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support(), "\n",
    "sink.number() :", sink.number(), "\n",
    "isatty(stdout()) :", isatty(stdout())
  )
}
```

Building error this way, `sink.number > 0` so result is not TRUE even in RStudio


```r
er <- errorCondition(
  message = crayon_sitrep())
stop(er)
```

```
## Error: 
##  crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() : TRUE 
##  sink.number() : 1 
##  isatty(stdout()) : FALSE
```

However, using a specific class for a condition and definining a special method
for `conditionMessage`, `sink.number()` is equal to 0 (reset ?) and `has_color` 
see RStudio is used. That why we get TRUE for color support. 


```r
conditionMessage.barfoo <- function(c) crayon_sitrep()
stop(errorCondition("", class = "barfoo"))
```

```
## Error: 
##  crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() : TRUE 
##  sink.number() : 0 
##  isatty(stdout()) : FALSE
```

## With rlang

This above is causing issue with rlang error too,and thus the tidyverse in
Rmarkdown.


```r
rlang::abort(crayon_sitrep())
```

```
## Error: 
##  crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() : TRUE 
##  sink.number() : 1 
##  isatty(stdout()) : FALSE
```


```r
conditionMessage.foobar <- function(cnd) crayon_sitrep()
rlang::abort(.subclass = "foobar")
```

```
## Error: 
##  crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() : TRUE 
##  sink.number() : 0 
##  isatty(stdout()) : FALSE
```

</details>

I think `has_color()` should always return FALSE when code is executed from an R markdown chunk using interactively `rmarkdown::render()`, `knitr::knit()` or non interactively using the Knit button.
Depending on their output format, user could opt-in as they wish (see https://github.com/r-lib/crayon/issues/24#issuecomment-581068792 for html output for example)

The checks about `sink` should have been enough but it seems that it is not, due to this special behavioir in `conditionMessage`. 🤷‍♂ 

Could be related in a way to r-lib/crayon#80 but seems different.

title: Detection of colour in non-interactive RStudio session
description:
`has_color()` returns `TRUE` within non-interactive RStudio:

```r
# Within RStudio:
callr::r(function() crayon::has_color())
#> [1] TRUE

# Outside RStudio:
callr::r(function() crayon::has_color())
#> [1] FALSE
```

I think this is because the `rstudio_with_ansi_support()` check comes before the `isatty()` check:

```r
# Within RStudio:
callr::r(function() crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() && sink.number() == 0)
#> [1] TRUE
callr::r(function() isatty(stdout()))
#> [1] FALSE

# Outside RStudio:
callr::r(function() crayon:::rstudio_with_ansi_support() && sink.number() == 0)
#> [1] FALSE
callr::r(function() isatty(stdout()))
#> [1] FALSE
```

Happy to send a PR to inverse the branches if that diagnostic looks right.

title: Should has_color return TRUE if stderr is a tty?
description:
Currently `has_color()` checks if `stdout()` is a tty, and if it is not then colors are disabled.

https://github.com/r-lib/crayon/blob/84be62074ad5b3ede54dd035ef4003f808f34f12/R/has_color.r#L64

However it is possible users would still want color if stdout is redirected (so is no longer a tty) but stderr is still a tty and the colors are being used in messages to stderr. In fact perhaps it is actually more common for colors to be used in output to stderr than stdout?

I am not sure how best to address this, as crayon has no way of knowing where the output is going to, but the current behavior seems too conservative.

title: Better detection in various RStudio sessions
description:
This detection is triggered if `RSTUDIO` is set.

There are a number of cases:

- [ ] 1. Console.
- [ ] 2. R process started from console, via `callr::r` or `system`, etc.
- [ ] 3. Terminal.
- [ ] 4. R subprocess started from an R process in the RStudio terminal.
- [ ] 5. Build pane.
- [ ] 6. R subprocess of an R process in the build pane.

We do not deal with the cases where a terminal app (xterm) or another RStudio process is started from within RStudio, as these cases are not very common.

In general also need to check for `RSTUDIO_CONSOLE_COLOR`, because if it is not set, then RStudio does not support colors, anywhere.

An additional difficulty is that when RStudio starts up, many of its informative environment variables are not yet set, so we need to be careful in this case.

We will also cache the detection, and use it, unless a `sink()` is active.

## Solutions:

### 1. Console.

`isatty(stdout()) == FALSE` but `rstudioapi::isAvailable() == TRUE`. Need special case at startup time.

### 2. R process started from console, via `callr::r` or `system`, etc.

`isatty(stdout()) == FALSE`, and `rstudioapi::isAvailable() == FALSE`. `RSTUDIO_TERM` is not set.

### 3. Terminal.

`RSTUDIO_TERM` is set. `isatty(stdout()) == TRUE`.

### 4. R subprocess started from an R process in the RStudio terminal.

`RSTUDIO_TERM` is set, but `isatty(stdout()) == FALSE`.

### 5. Build pane.

???

### 6. R subprocess of an R process in the build pane.

???

```
> options(crayon.enabled = TRUE)
> tibble(x = 1:5, y = 1, z = x ^ 2 + y)
[90m# A tibble: 5 x 3[39m
      x     y     z
  [3m[90m<int>[39m[23m [3m[90m<dbl>[39m[23m [3m[90m<dbl>[39m[23m
[90m1[39m     1     1     2
[90m2[39m     2     1     5
[90m3[39m     3     1    10
[90m4[39m     4     1    17

> tibble(x = 1:5, y = 1, z = x ^ 2 + y)
# A tibble: 5 x 3
      x     y     z
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     1     2
2     2     1     5
3     3     1    10
4     4     1    17
5     5     1    26
```

in Rgui on Windows. I tracked the issue back to the fact that if you launch Rgui from the Start Menu or Windows command prompt, you get:

```R
> crayon::has_color()
[1] FALSE
```

but if you launch Rgui from ConEmu, you get:

```R
> crayon::has_color()
[1] TRUE
```

even though you actually don't have color support. Setting `option(crayon.enabled = FALSE)` solves the problem but it's sufficiently conditional as to be confusing.

I guess the issue is that this line: https://github.com/r-lib/crayon/blob/3e751fbff44896abcd5e58eac37655564b61c22c/R/has_color.r#L68 is `TRUE` in both cases because the R session inherits the ConEmu environment variables.

A possible way to distinguish would be to grab:

```R
> .Platform$GUI
[1] "Rgui"
```

versus

```R
> .Platform$GUI
[1] "RTerm"
```

and then only enable crayon  `if (.Platform$GUI == "RTerm" && Sys.getenv("ConEmuANSI") == "ON")`.

As a reference, session info is the same in both instances:

title: Export crayon:::is_r_color and crayon:::style_from_r_color?
description:
Thanks for the amazing package!

A new package [`multicolor`](https://github.com/aedobbyn/multicolor) makes heavy use of `crayon`. There is a [PR](https://github.com/sckott/cowsay/pull/59#issuecomment-407264843) for it to be integrated into the [`cowsay`](https://github.com/sckott/cowsay) package by @sckott and friends.

A new `cowsay` release to CRAN would also require that `multicolor` be on CRAN. Currently `multicolor` uses two internal `crayon` functions, [`is_r_color`](https://github.com/aedobbyn/multicolor/blob/master/R/multi_color.R#L64) and [`style_from_r_color`](https://github.com/aedobbyn/multicolor/blob/master/R/utils.R#L33) and so wouldn't pass a CRAN check. 

Would it be possible to export these two functions in the next release of `crayon`? If you'd rather not export and have other ideas I'd be totally open to them. `is_r_color` would be feasible to copy the code for, but `style_from_r_color` wouldn't be, imo.

title: CLI capabilities detection does not respect the active app
description:
The package offers a number of functions to detect the CLI capabilities, however, it is not straightforward to detect the capabilities of the *active* output connection. For instance, in my scripts I usually set the cli output to `stdout` (makes it easier to capture output):

     cli::start_app(output = "stdout")

In real usage, `stdout` may be proper terminal output, or it could be redirected to a file or another app. Being able to detect the capability of the actual output connection is important here, as the script could adjust it's output appropriately (e.g. avoid using animations when we are redirecting the output to the file). 

Hovewer, `cli_output_connection()` still returns the default `stderr` so functions like `is_ansi_tty()` and `is_dynamic_tty()` do not work out of box. Even more, they still don't work if you do  something like `is_dynamic_tty(default_app()$output)`, since they expect a connection object and not a string. Now, the following does works

    is_dynamic_tty(cli::: get_real_output(default_app()$output))

but its unnecessary verbose and relies on internal package symbols. 

My suggestion to improve this:

- either change `cli_output_connection()` to respect the default app (might be a breaking change though)
- patch  `is_ansi_tty()`, `is_dynamic_tty()` etc. to work with string stream descriptions (hooking in `get_real_output()`)

title: Pluralization with empty last alternative produces the wrong output
description:
I have a slightly odd use case where I was trying to "pluralize" the verb exist and ran into the an issue where `{?s/}` is being treated as `{?s}`.

```r
vars = c("X")
cli::cli_text("{vars} exist{?s/}")
#> X exist
cli::cli_text("{vars} exist{?s}") 
#> X exist

vars = c("X","Y")
cli::cli_text("{vars} exist{?s/}")
#> X and Y exists
cli::cli_text("{vars} exist{?s}") 
#> X and Y exists
```

it seems like this may be a more general issue with a trailing empty alternative:

```r
vars = c()
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/C}") # Ok
#> wordA
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?/B/C}")  # Ok
#> word
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A//C}")  # Ok
#> wordA
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/}")  # Wrong
#> wordB

vars = c("X")
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/C}") # Ok
#> X wordB
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?/B/C}")  # Ok
#> X wordB
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A//C}")  # Ok
#> X word
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/}")  # Wrong
#> X wordA

vars = c("X","Y")
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/C}") # Ok
#> X and Y wordC
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?/B/C}")  # Ok
#> X and Y wordC
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A//C}")  # Ok
#> X and Y wordC
cli::cli_text("{vars} word{?A/B/}")  # Wrong
#> X and Y wordB
```

title: Expose or repackage useful formatters (e.g. pluralization)
description:
I didn't see this in an existing issue, but apologies if it's been discussed already.

```r
cli::cli_text("time: {x} year{?s}")
```

is an extremely useful piece of code but it's limited to console output (unless I'm mistaken). It would be more widely beneficial to either export a function which produces the text as a string before going to `cat()`, PR such a helper to `{glue}`, or create a helper package which `{cli}` could import.

It seems odd if one needs to use `capture.output()` on this to make use of it outside of a console.

title: Rules in ASCII
description:
I'm not sure this is an issue, but I wanted to share it because it seems a bit strange.

I've been working on making skimr tests pass under testthat 3 which means that they match the output for `cli.unicode=FALSE`.  This impacted two things, ellipsis and rules. The ellipses was fine once I figured out that sometimes it is "~" and sometimes "...".

In terms of rules this file passes.
https://github.com/ropensci/skimr/blob/master/tests/testthat/dplyr/filter-skim.txt

You can see that the rendering is slightly different when it is a plain rule versus one with text.

```
-- Data Summary ------------------------
                           Values
Name                       iris  
Number of rows             150   
Number of columns          5     
_______________________ 
```
It's a subtle difference that did require me to change a lot of tests, but more important it's not what I would expect if I were rendering in the console.

If you think this is an issue you can see our code that uses cli in this file.
https://github.com/ropensci/skimr/blob/76d59f3c0424eccad272502d18c5d64f5974d3af/R/skim_print.R

title: cli_verbatim does not respect margins
description:
Not sure if this is a bug, but if a container has defined margins/padding, only the first verbatim line respects those. An example:

    cli_div(theme = list(.block = list("margin-left" = 4)))
    cli_verbatim("hello", "hello")  

outputs

        hello
    hello

In contrast, 

    cli_div(theme = list(.block = list("margin-left" = 4)))
    cli_verbatim("hello")
    cli_verbatim("hello")

outputs 

        hello
        hello

which seems counter-intuitive behavior to me. 

If this is working as intended, is there a supported way of outputting multiple lines of pre-formatted text (without glue interpolation) while respecting the margins?

title: [Feature Proposal] Convert R function to cli program
description:
It would be nice if there was an easy way to augment a single R function responsible for a CLI with a parser so that it can be run from the command line.

This may be out of scope for this package - although I think this feature is too small to be its own package.  Would you consider adding a function -> CLI program conversion function (possibly powered by [argparser](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/argparser/index.html)), alternatively this function could be a better fit for that package. My thought is something that converts

```r
main <- function(input = "/home/me/", out = "/home/you/"){
  # awesome cli code
}
```

into

```r
library(argparser)

args <- 
  arg_parser("main") %>%
  add_argument("input", default = "/home/me/") %>%
  add_argument("output", default = "/home/you/") %>%
  parse_args()

main(input = args$input, output = args$output)
```

The naive version would be easy enough to write. Because of R's amazing reflection capabilities we can inspect on the formals of the function to get argument names and defaults.  Although constraining and or coercing the input types might be subtle. 

Let me know if this is of interest, and I can open a WIP PR.

title: Support for "Doing X... done" messages
description:
Would it make sense to add a function that prints `Doing X... done` messages to the console? 

That is, a user-provided expression is evaluated together with printing the `Doing X...` message to the console (without the newline!). Then depending on whether an exception occured or not, `done\n` or `fail\n` is printed.

Usually a call to `message(..., appendLF = FALSE)` or `cat(..., file = stderr())` plus wrapping the expression with `tryCatch()` does the job, but perhaps it'd be a good idea to automate this. Or at least to add an `appendLF` flag to the `cat_*` functions.

First of all thank you for this wonderful tool 💪

``` r
#> 2019-08-29 11:13:01
cli::cat_rule(Sys.time())
```

title: Is cli.width an appropriate default width for rule* functions?
description:
Editors other than RStudio have console windows that can have line truncation dynamically toggled, and can be scrolled horizontally as well as vertically. This can be utilised to set a large value for the `cli.width` option and have R output print without columns getting moved onto new lines or getting removed altogether (like with Tibbles).

Using this setting creates an annoyance though with packages that use the `cli::rule` function since they may print many thousands of useless `-` or `=` characters to the console. E.g.

![cli_rule](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9996346/46184862-d4b50800-c31a-11e8-9eb6-4e04fc019c03.png)

Could `console_width()` look for some other option in preference to `cli.width`? maybe `cli.visible.width` or `rule.width`?

Edit: The major annoyance actually comes in running `testthat`, where the frequent use of `rule` in the output seems to slow everything down.

```
├─R6 (2.2.2)
├─selectr (0.4-1)
│ ├─xml2 (1.2.0)
│ │ ├─magrittr (1.5)
│ │ └─Rcpp (0.12.18)
│ ├─stringr (1.3.1)
│ │ ├─glue (1.3.0)

│ │ │ │ └─withr (2.1.2)
```

> `knitr:::is_latex_output()`. This function was exported recently in the devel version of knitr.

Should we work along these lines? Or should knitr (or even the user) just set the `cli.unicode` option?

title: ruler()
description:
Not sure if this should be exported or not but it's sometimes useful for debugging

```R
ruler <- function(width = console_width()) {
  x <- seq_len(width)
  y <- rep("-", length(x))

  y[x %% 5 == 0] <- "+"
  y[x %% 10 == 0] <- crayon::bold(as.character((x[x %% 10 == 0] %/% 10) %% 10))

  cat(y, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(x %% 10, "\n", sep = "")
}
```
